papers.title: Virtual Reality to Reduce Anxiety in Veterans Undergoing Chemotherapy Infusions.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Veterans are predisposed to generalized anxiety, and a cancer diagnosis can intensify psychological distress and overall unpleasant experiences during treatment. Infusion clinic staff at a veterans hospital tend to focus care primarily on the medical needs of patients, but evidence suggests health outcomes improve when both the mental health and physical needs of patients with cancer are addressed. OBJECTIVES: This evidence-based practice project sought to reduce anxiety in veterans undergoing chemotherapy infusions through virtual reality (VR) meditation. METHODS: The Iowa Model of Evidence-Based Practice guided the project. A literature search and appraisal identified level I-III evidence suggesting that VR meditation, compared to standard care, had significant reduction of anxiety in patients with cancer undergoing chemotherapy. At a veterans hospital outpatient infusion clinic, a team developed a standard operating procedure, trained nursing staff, and administered immersive VR meditation via headset with an installed meditation application during chemotherapy infusions. Participants (N = 17) completed pre- and postintervention surveys measuring anxiety. FINDINGS: Results suggested a statistically significant reduction in anxiety from pre-VR meditation (mean = 1.59) to post-VR meditation (mean = 0.18) (p = 0.003). Nursing implementation of VR meditation during chemotherapy infusions may reduce anxiety in patients with cancer undergoing chemotherapy.

papers.title: Prenatal Education Strategies Designed to Support Women's Mobility During Labor: A Scoping Review.
papers.abstract: AIM: To identify prenatal education strategies that support women's mobility during labor and to examine how these strategies address childbirth self-efficacy and informed decision-making as complementary capabilities relevant to active participation during labor. METHODS: A scoping review (updated October 12, 2025) searched six bibliographic databases and one gray-literature database using predefined eligibility criteria. Studies on prenatal education that addressed women's preparation for mobility and upright positions during labor, including related dimensions of decision-making and self-efficacy, were included. Screening and data extraction were performed independently in duplicate, with consensus procedures. Findings are presented narratively and in tables/figures. RESULTS: Thirty articles were included, predominantly primary studies (n = 27; 90.0%). The review identified 15 studies that explicitly operationalized mobility/upright positions as a structured, primary strategy, alongside additional studies that mentioned mobility without a structured focus. Three specific strategies to promote active labor were described: a birth ball exercise program, the Labor Hopscotch Framework, and birth plan counseling. Practices such as yoga, mindfulness, and experiential/discovery-based learning addressed body awareness, connections between movement and fetal positioning, and women's comfort and confidence through active engagement. CONCLUSION: Despite recommendations to inform expectant women about active-labor options in prenatal education, relatively few studies provided structured, mobility-focused strategies. Where present, studies reported greater childbirth confidence, use of non-pharmacological pain relief, lower pain, and increased use of upright positions. A persistent research gap remains regarding targeted prenatal education that prepares women to make informed choices about mobility and positioning during labor.

papers.title: Implementation Evaluation of CALM Care: Examining a Universal Procedural Care Approach for Healthcare Workers in a Tertiary Paediatric Hospital Setting.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Children experience procedural trauma from medical interventions that may cause harm. Yet, healthcare workers report limited access to relevant training. CALM Care (Comfort, Analgesia, Language, Mindfulness, Memory) is a trauma-informed model and training approach for universal best-practice procedural care. AIM: (1) Examine how CALM Care is implemented in real-world settings, (2) generate knowledge about how multi-modal implementation strategies influence uptake, (3) pilot measures of clinical effectiveness. DESIGN: Mixed-methods implementation evaluation. METHODS: CALM Care was implemented across eight departments (~480 staff) within a metropolitan paediatric teaching hospital between October 2024 and June 2025, guided by the integrated Promoting Action of Research Implementation in Health Services framework. Implementation strategies (e.g., facilitation) were informed by programme theory. Structured observations (N = 63) of children (mean age 2 years, 7 months) undergoing needling was used to assess fidelity, acceptability and clinical outcomes. Organisational metadata informed adoption and feasibility. Data was analysed using a deductive-inductive hybrid thematic approach. RESULTS: Seven departments participated. Following implementation, CALM Care principles (except Comfort) were adopted (i.e., > 20% increased use in standard care). Up to 80% of targeted staff (n = 360) completed training. Documentation of procedural plans increased six-fold. First-attempt proceduralist success improved > 10%, although pain scores did not clinically change significantly. Acceptability to staff and consumer satisfaction was high. Fidelity was strongest for Language (95%), Mindfulness (95%) and Analgesia (85%). Key enablers were adaptability of CALM Care operationalisation, leadership engagement and integration of context-specific resources and workflows. CONCLUSIONS: Theoretically informed strategies support adoption of trauma-minimising practices. However, sustained leadership and policy support are essential to maintain cultural change. IMPLICATIONS FOR PROFESSION AND/OR PATIENT CARE: Organisational adoption of CALM Care may enable delivery of least-restrictive care to reduce medical trauma in paediatric hospital settings. REPORTING METHOD: The evaluation followed the StaRI and TIDieR checklists. PATIENT OR PUBLIC CONTRIBUTION: No Patient or Public Contribution: Patients or members of the public were not involved in the design, conduct, reporting, or dissemination plans of this research, which has been acknowledged as a limitation of this study. GLOBAL CONTRIBUTION: Dynamic facilitation that builds workforce confidence in procedural care may shape a child's lifelong engagement with healthcare. CALM Care, every time, matters.
